text:
Avrith c. Ayoub

2011 QCCQ 339

COURT OF QUEBEC

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

TOWN OF

MONTREAL

Civil Division

No:

500-22-141025-075

DATE:

January 20, 2011

______________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

SUZANNE HANDMAN, J.C.Q.

______________________________________________________________________

SEYMOUR AVRITH

Plaintiff

v.

PAUL AYOUB

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Seymour Avrith is claiming $24,000 as damages
from Paul Ayoub for defamation. Mr. Avrith alleges that Mr. Ayoub attacked his
reputation by filing a complaint before the Quebec Bar Association, which was
without merit, and by maliciously accusing Mr. Avrith of lying in Court.
Defendant denies the claim.

THE QUESTIONS IN LITIGATION:

[
2
]

The Court must determine if the remarks made by
Mr. Ayoub to the Bar AssocIation and to the Court were defamatory and if he
committed a wrongful act. In the affirmative, the Court must decide whether Mr.
Avrith suffered damages, entitling him to compensation.

THE EVIDENCE:

[
3
]

The parties met in 1996. Mr. Ayoub, who was
seeking commercial space for his clothing store, Les Modes J.M., rented a space
from Phillip Avrith Investment Inc.. The company was represented by Seymour
Avrith and as a result, Mr. Ayoub dealt with Seymour Avrith with respect to his
lease and any ensuing problems.

[
4
]

The lease, which began in May 1996, was extended
on several occasions. The last extension took place in 2000 when the parties
signed a five-year lease.

[
5
]

During the time Phillip Avrith Investments Inc.
owned the property in question, Seymour Avrith, an attorney, acted as the
property manager for Phillip Avrith Investment. He took care of all aspects of
the administration, including collection and leasing as well as the acquisition
and sale of properties.

[
6
]

His role as administrator, which began in 1996,
continued until 2005, with the exception of several months in 2002 when his
brother Phillip took over the administration. Tenants were advised by a letter,
dated October 17, 2002, that Seymour Avrith's functions were suspended. Mr.
Avrith explained that this letter only affected his authority to collect
rent.

[
7
]

Seymour Avrith later resumed his duties. The
tenants were not informed of his return in writing. According to Mr. Avrith,
the parties reverted to their way of functioning and the tenants, including Mr.
Ayoub, were aware of this fact.

[
8
]

Initially, the relationship between Seymour
Avrith and Paul Ayoub was very good; the two got together regularly for coffee.
Issues then arose because of an alleged lack of heat in the premises. Mr. Ayoub
testified that the heating equipment was inadequate; his store and his office
were unbearably cold.

[
9
]

In January 2004, Phillip Avrith Investment
instituted an action against Les Modes J. M. for unpaid taxes and heating
costs, which was later settled out of Court.

[
10
]

On January 14, 2005, Mr. Ayoub requested an
extension of the lease. Because of problems relating to heating and taxes,
Phillip Avrith Investment decided that its tenants, Mr. Ayoub and Les Modes
M.J., posed too many problems and refused to extend the lease. Mr. Avrith
considered that the ensuing problems resulted from this refusal.

[
11
]

On February 23, 2005, Les Modes J.M. demanded
proper heating equipment be installed. It claimed damages for the loss of
sales, due to the lack of heat. It then instituted an action in damages on
March 10, 2005, against Phillip Avrith Investments in Small Claims Court,
alleging heating insufficiencies.

[
12
]

Hearings were held on November 13, 2006 and on
February 19, 2007. After the November hearing, during which Mr. Avrith declared
he was an administrator of Phillip Avrith Investment, Mr. Ayoub filed a
complaint with the Quebec Bar Association, alleging that Mr. Avrith had falsely
presented himself as an administrator of his brother's company.

[
13
]

On November 24, 2006, the Bar Association
advised Mr. Avrith of Mr. Ayoub's complaint. Seymour Avrith was shocked; he
declared he would never lie.

[
14
]

On April 23, 2007, the Bar Association dismissed
the complaint, concluding that Me Avrith had not lied to the Court during the
November 13th hearing.

[
15
]

Prior to the Bar's decision, the hearing
continued before the Honourable Diane Quenneville. According to Mr.
Avrith, during the hearing, Mr. Ayoub declared Seymour Avrith had lied to the
Court during the previous hearing, by stating that he, Seymour Avrith, was the
administrator of the properties.

[
16
]

Mr. Avrith testified that Mr. Ayoub knew that
he, Seymour Avrith, was the administrator of his brother's business, Phillip
Avrith Investment. When Mr. Ayoub accused him of lying, the Courtroom was full.

[
17
]

Mr. Avrith testified that, although he is not a
director or an officer, he acted on behalf of Phillip Avrith Investment. He
took care of the administration of its properties and, as such, he was the
administrator or manager of the company.

[
18
]

Mr. Avrith is holding Mr. Ayoub responsible for all
the damages resulting from Mr. Ayoub's unfounded complaint before the Bar and
his statement in Court alleging that he, Seymour Avrith, had lied. For Mr.
Avrith, Mr. Ayoub attacked his reputation and his integrity; his reputation
being his most valuable asset.

[
19
]

He points to the fact he is a member of the
Quebec Bar Association, a governor and benefactor of the Institut de
cardiologie de Montréal, founder of Mount Sinai Hospital, and a donor of the
Canadian Jewish Association and Cleveland Hospital. Mr. Avrith is seeking
$19,000 as moral damages and $5,000 as punitive damages.

ANALYSIS:

The Applicable Legal Principles
:

[
20
]

Any attack on one's reputation, whether it be
verbal or in writing, injurious or defamatory, constitutes a fault, which, if
it entails damages, is sanctioned by monetary compensation
[1]
.

[
21
]

An action in defamation is based on the ordinary
rules of civil liability; the element of wrongdoing is appreciated according to
the general criteria of
article 1457
of the
Civil code of Quebec
:

Every person has a duty to abide by
the rules of conduct which lie upon him, according to the circumstances usage
or law, so as not to cause injury to another.

(…)

[
22
]

Accordingly, a plaintiff must establish by
preponderant evidence the existence of injury, of a wrongful act and a causal
connection between the two.

[
23
]

To demonstrate the existence of injury, the
written or spoken remarks must be defamatory, that is their communication must
cause someone to lose in estimation or consideration or prompt unfavourable or
unpleasant feelings toward him or her
[2]
.

[
24
]

As explained by the Supreme Court in the
case of
Prud'homme
vs
Prud'homme
[3]
,
an objective standard is applied to determine whether remarks are defamatory:
“We must ask
whether an ordinary person would believe that the remarks made, when viewed as
a whole, brought discredit on the reputation of another person.”

[
25
]

Words may be defamatory not only because of the
idea conveyed but also by the insinuations that may be inferred from them.

[
26
]

In order for defamation to give rise to an action
in damages, its author must have committed a wrongful act. This wrongful act
can result from two types of conduct, one being malicious and the other merely
negligent.

[
27
]

The first is an act in which the defendant
knowingly, in bad faith and with the intent to harm, attacks the reputation of
the victim and seeks to ridicule, humiliate or expose him to the hatred or
contempt of the public or a group. The second results from behaviour in which
there is no intent to harm but the defendant has nevertheless attacked the
victim's reputation by his recklessness, his negligence, his impertinence or
his carelessness. Both types of behaviour constitute a fault.

[
28
]

As the Supreme Court explained in
Prud'homme

vs
Prud'homme
, a person who makes defamatory remarks could be civilly
liable in three situations:

(1)        A person makes
unpleasant remarks about another knowing them to be false; the intention is to
harm.

(2)        A person spreads
unpleasant things about another when he should have known them to be false.

(3)        A scandalmonger makes
unfavourable but true statements about another person without any valid reason
for doing so.

[
29
]

Determining fault is a question of fact, which
is analyzed taking into account the context and the circumstances in which the
remarks were made as well as the need to reconcile two fundamental values, that
of freedom of expression and the right to one's reputation.

The complaint before the Quebec Bar
Association
:

[
30
]

Mr. Avrith claims that Mr. Ayoub's unnecessary
and unlawful attack on Mr. Avrith's reputation and integrity before the
Quebec Bar caused him damages, for which he is entitled to receive
compensation.

[
31
]

Les Modes J. M. instituted an action against
Philip Avrith Investments Inc. before Small Claims Court on March 5, 2005.
During the hearing on November 13, 2006, the following exchange took place:

“Mr. Ayoub: you (inaudible) …as a
lawyer, you're not supposed to be here

Mr. Avrith: I'm not here as a
lawyer…

(…)

The Court: Just a minute. You're
mister?

Mr. Avrith: Avrith

(…)

Mr. Avrith: I am the administrator
of this company from nineteen ninety-four (1994). I signed the leases
personally with this gentleman for the last twelve (12) years, I met with him
and discussed these leases.”

[
32
]

Mr. Avrith asked that the case be dismissed,
alleging that the issue of damages had already been settled by a previous case
between the same parties. The objection, based on the principle of
“chose jugée”
was taken under advisement and ultimately rejected by judgment
rendered on December 15, 2006.

[
33
]

In the interim, on November 15, 2006, Mr. Ayoub
submitted the following complaint to the Office of the Syndic of the Quebec Bar
Association:

“On 13 of November 2006 I have a
case with his brother Phillip Avrith Investments in Small Claim Cour Mr Seymour
Avrith present himself as administrater (sic) to the company of his brother
whis (sic) it is false.”

[
34
]

The Syndic, after receiving written explanations
from Mr. Avrith and having taken cognizance of the lease between the parties,
noted that Seymour Avrith is mentioned on the lease as the duly authorized
representative of Philippe Avrith Investments Inc. and is a signatory of the
lease.

[
35
]

The Syndic concluded as follows:

“Under the circumstances, we cannot
conclude that Me Avrith lied to the court during the hearing of November 13,
2006. Consequently, we do not plan to lay a disciplinary complaint against him
and we will close the file.”

[
36
]

Counsel for Mr. Avrith contends Mr. Avrith never
said he was a director or officer of the company and he did not make a false
statement to the Court. He submits that there was no basis for Mr. Ayoub's
complaint against Mr. Avrith before the Bar. For Mr. Avrith, the complaint
was malicious; Mr. Ayoub acted out of spite and revenge, when his lease was not
extended.

[
37
]

The Court considers that the remarks contained
in Mr. Ayoub's complaint before the Bar Association are, in fact, defamatory.
They discredit Mr. Avrith in that they put into question his honesty.

[
38
]

This brings us to the question of whether Mr.
Ayoub was justified in presenting a complaint to the Bar against Mr. Avrith,
alleging that he had made a false statement in Court. In other words, did Mr.
Ayoub commit a wrongful act?

[
39
]

According to Mr. Ayoub, when the parties
appeared in Small Claims Court, Mr. Avrith failed to present a resolution,
a mandate or power of attorney, establishing his status to represent Phillip
Avrith Investments at the hearing. However, it should be noted that the
proceedings in Small Claims Court are not as strict as the regular division.

[
40
]

Mr. Ayoub maintains there is no basis to say
that his complaint before the Bar is unfounded. The copy of a CIDREX attached
to his complaint does not list Seymour Avrith as an
“administrateur”
of the company.

[
41
]

It is true that Mr. Avrith was not an
administrator within the legal or the French meaning of the term
“administrateur”. He was not a director or an officer of Phillip Avrith
Investments. However, he managed the company and in the English language, the
usual term for a person who occupies such a function is either a manager or an
administrator. Accordingly, it is not false for Mr. Avrith to have stated that
he was the administrator of his brother's business.

[
42
]

It is also not erroneous for Mr. Ayoub to state
that Mr. Avrith is not an “administrateur”. As indicated above, the status of
Mr. Avrith, as administrator of Phillip Avrith Investments, varies
depending on which language is used.

[
43
]

However, Mr. Ayoub invoked that Mr. Avrith made
a false statement by saying he was an administrator, based on the French
meaning of the term
“administrateur”
, when
the parties communicated with each other in English.

[
44
]

While the Court does not consider that Mr.
Ayoub's complaint contained malicious language, there does not appear to be any
valid reason for him to have submitted a complaint to the Bar Association. His
actions are unjustified.

[
45
]

There remains the question of damages. The
criteria for evaluating compensatory damages have been established in many
cases, as follows
[4]
:

1) la gravité intrinsèque de
l'acte;

2) sa portée particulière sur celui
qui en a été la victime;

3) l'importance de la diffusion;

4) l'identité des personnes qui en
ont pris connaissance et les effets que ces propos ont provoqués chez ces
personnes;

5) le degré de déchéance plus ou
moins considérable à laquelle la diffamation a réduit la victime par
comparaison à son statut antérieur;

6) la durée raisonnablement
prévisible du dommage cuasé et de la déchéance subie;

7) la contribution possible de la
victime par sa conduite ou ses attitudes et;

8) les circonstances extérieures
qui, de toute façon et indépendamment de l'acte fautif, constituent des causes
probables du préjudice allégué ou de partie de ce préjudice.

[
46
]

In the present case, as indicated above, after
Mr. Ayoub's complaint was submitted to the Bar Association, the Syndic obtained
Mr. Avrith's version of the facts and concluded that the complaint was
unfounded. It advised the parties that it did not plan to lay a disciplinary
complaint against Mr. Avrith and closed its file.

[
47
]

There was no publicity or diffusion of Mr.
Ayoub's letter to the Bar. The correspondence is confidential and, in fact, no
one other than the parties themselves and the Syndic were aware of the
complaint.

[
48
]

While Mr. Avrith testified at great length as to
the fact that his reputation is his greatest asset, he has not shown how his
reputation has been affected. Mr. Avrith has not lost his status as a member in
good standing with the Quebec Bar Association; his reputation has not been
discredited in the eyes of the Bar Association or in the eyes of this Court.

[
49
]

In sum, there have not been any consequences
following the complaint and Mr. Avrith has not established that he
suffered any damages.

[
50
]

As for the claim for punitive damages, in the
absence of any evidence of an intentional and illicit violation within the
meaning of
section 49
of the
Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
[5]
, no such damages are awarded.

The
remarks made in Court
:

[
51
]

Mr. Avrith contends that Mr. Ayoub knowingly
defamed him in Small Claims Court during the hearing held on February 19, 2007,
by stating that he, Mr. Avrith, had lied to the Court in the previous hearing.

[
52
]

The treatment of defamation in the context of
legal proceedings has been considered by the Courts in a number of judgments.
In the case of
Terreault
c.
Bigras
[6]
,
cited in
Gagn
é c.
Galland
[7]
, the
Court of Appeal held that five elements must be proven to establish the
defamation in the context of legal proceedings:

1)
that the allegations are defamatory

2)
that they are false

3)
that they were not pertinent to the litigation in question

4)
that there was no reasonable motive to make them

5)
that they are malicious or reckless to the point of being malicious.

[
53
]

According to the authors J.-L. Baudouin and P.
Deslauriers
[8]
:

« Une saine administration de
la justice impose qu'un témoin dans une instance judiciaire, puisse parler en
toute franchise sans crainte de se voir subséquemment recherché en dommage pour
les paroles prononcées par lui. »

[
54
]

The Court in the case of
Gagné
c.
Galand
[9]
noted a number of facts
that apply in Small Claims Division which are distinct from the regular
division:

-           les parties ne sont pas
représentées par avocat, tel qu'édicté à l'article 955 C.p.c. (sauf exception à
l'article 977.1 C.p.c.);

-           généralement, c'est le
juge qui pose les questions au témoin (article 976 C.p.c.). On voit à cet article
que le juge mène le débat, posant à l'occasion des questions ouvertes, comme on
peut le voir à la transcription P-5, par exemple: « Quelle est votre
version des faits? »

-           Il n'y a pas de
procédure préliminaire ni de divulgation préalable des documents à produire
alors que, dans le régime général de la procédure civile (pour les créances
autres que des petites créances), cela permet parfois d'identifier et
d'éliminer dès le départ des allégations calomnieuses, diffamatoires out
totalement dénuées de pertinence.

[
55
]

The Court, in the above-cited case, considered
that it was contrary to the proper administration of justice to subject an
unrepresented litigant, in Small Claims Court, to the same standards of
wrongdoing, in the case of defamation, as a litigant who had retained the
services of a lawyer. Accordingly, an individual complaining of defamation,
having occurred during a Small Claims Division hearing, must demonstrate by
convincing evidence the malice or malicious recklessness on the part of the
author of the alleged defamatory remarks.

[
56
]

In the present case, during the hearing held
before the Honourable Diane Quenneville on February 19, 2007, Mr. Avrith
wished to postpone the case because of the complaint that Mr. Ayoub had filed
against him before the Bar Association. The following exchange took place
between the parties and the Court:

“
Mr. Avrith
: It's been
decided. I abide by the decision of the Court. What I want to get to, Your
Ladyship, is the question…is that following that decision…before the decision
was rendered,
Mr. Ayoub went to the Bar Association and leveled a charge
against me
in effect
that I'm a liar
or whatever, whatever the
charge was.

The Court:  A liar or a lawyer?

Mr. Avrith: A liar.

The Court: A liar, oh.

Mr. Avrith
:
Yes, He says I lied to the Court
. Now, why…my first
argument here before the Court is that he leveled that charge. It's an
important charge to me personally. I am with the Bar forty-five years (45)
years in good standing without incident. So, I made a request to the Court and
to Mr. Ayoub that: why don't we wait for the decision of the Bar before we
proceed? And I have other grounds to ask for the postponement is that,
secondly, he has more than five (5) employees and…

(…)

The Court: You're asking for a
postponement this morning?

Mr. Avrith: Yes

(…)

The Court: Okay…I'm assuming you're
contesting the postponement?

Mr. Ayoub: That's right, because on
that date in November, when we appeared in front of the judge of the court, Mr.
Seymour Avrith presented himself as an administrator of the company. Then I
find out he's not an administrator, he's not supposed to be here that day in
November. That's why I had to go to the Barreau, because he lied to the judge.
He's not supposed to be an administrator of the company.

(…)

The Court: So you were saying that
a complaint was filed at the Bar against you.

Mr. Avrith: yes.

The Court: by Mr. Ayoub

Mr. Avrith: Yes, yes. I mean, it's
admitted by him in the proceedings, he filed it before Mr. Bilodeau, the
Assistant Syndic. And I just recently spoke to him and he says that he didn't
arrive at a decision, he needs a few other documents (inaudible) proceedings
and he'll arrive at a decision. So, I thought it appropriate, because it's a
very, to me personally, this is a very serious charge and has serious
consequences…

(…)

The Court: But the decision that
the Bar will render …has nothing to do with this case. I do not have…I'm not
bound…

(…)

The Court: And the criteria to rule
on this complaint are very much different than the matter I have in front of
me…So, I won't postpone for that matter.

(the underlining is ours)

[
57
]

Counsel Mr. Avrith claims that Mr. Ayoub's
remarks in Court constitute a second event and an aggravating factor.

[
58
]

The undersigned does not agree. Consider what
transpired at the hearing presided by Judge Quenneville and the context in
which the words were pronounced.

[
59
]

The transcript shows that Mr. Avrith wished to
obtain a postponement of the hearing. He raised the issue of the complaint
before the Bar; he also claimed that the number of persons employed by J. M.
Modes precluded it from instituting proceedings before the Small Claims Court.

[
60
]

However, it was Mr. Avrith, and not Mr. Ayoub,
who first raised the issue of the complaint in the hearing. Mr. Avrith declared
that Mr. Ayoub had complained to the Bar that he, Mr. Avrith, was a liar. Mr.
Ayoub then provided his explanation, in response to the request of the Court.
It was in this context that Mr. Ayoub pronounced the remarks, which Mr. Avrith
considers defamatory.

[
61
]

There was no need whatsoever for Mr. Avrith to
have mentioned the subject. As Judge Quenneville stated, the Court was not
concerned with the decision of the Syndic, which had nothing to do with the
case before it. The number of employees working for Les Modes J. M. was sufficient
to dispose of the action. Because Les Modes J. M. employs more than five (5)
people, the case was dismissed and the matter referred to the Civil Division of
the Court.

[
62
]

It should also be recalled that Mr. Ayoub, in
his complaint to the Bar, wrote that Mr. Avrith's claim of being an
administrator was “false”; he did not say Mr. Avrith was a liar. In Small
Claims Court, Mr. Ayoub, whose mother tongue is not English, responded to the
issue raised by Mr. Avrith and simply used the same terms as Mr. Avrith, namely
that Mr. Avrith “lied to the judge”.

[
63
]

Mr. Ayoub could reasonably have believed that
Judge Quenneville wanted to understand what the issue was before the Bar,
before she concluded that the complaint was not relevant to the case in the
Small Claims Division.

[
64
]

Furthermore, Mr. Ayoub was faced with a
representative from Phillip Avrith Investments who had legal training. Mr.
Ayoub was obviously trying to defend himself as well as he could. He considered
that Mr. Avrith should not be representing the company since he was not its
owner and, as a lawyer, he could not appear before that Court. The following
exchange took place during the first hearing in Small Claims Court on November
13, 2006, in which Mr. Ayoub attempted to disqualify Mr. Avrith:

“Mr. Ayoub: As a lawyer, you're not
supposed to be here.

Mr. Avrith: I'm not here as a
lawyer…

Mr. Ayoub: You're not the owner of
the building.

(…)

Mr. Avrith: It's a company that's
owned…that I used to (inaudible)…

Mr. Avrith: I'm sorry, Your Honour,
I can't pursue the case, I can't go against a lawyer.

The Court: Just a minute. You're
mister?

Mr. Avrith: Avrith

The Court: Avrith.

Avrith: I am the administrator of
this company from nineteen ninety-four (1994)…”

[
65
]

The Court stated in
Gagné
c.
Galland
[10]
, that those appearing before the Small
Claims Court should not be held to the same standard with respect to wrongdoing
as those assisted by an attorney and must be able to express themselves freely
and with frankness:

« Il serait contraire à la
saine administration de la justice qu'un justiciable, convoqué comme défendeur
en Cour des petites créances, mais sans avoir le droit à l'assistance d'un
avocat, soit astreint à une norme de faute en cas de diffamation, d'intensité
équivalant à celle d'un avocat ou d'un justiciable ayant retenu les services
d'un avocat.

De l'avis du Tribunal, en tel cas,
celui qui se plaint de diffamation durant une audience en Cour des petites
créances, doit réussir une preuve particulièrement convaincante quant à la
malice ou quant à la témérité malicieuse de l'auteur des propos diffamatoires.

Rappelons que le Tribunal doit
appliquer les règles de droit en tenant compte non seulement des paroles
prononcées mais aussi du contexte où ces paroles ont été prononcées.

(…)

Les gens doivent pouvoir venir s'exprimer
librement et franchement devant les tribunaux. »

[
66
]

Finally, the Court wishes to point out that
while Mr. Avrith accuses Mr. Ayoub of publicly saying that he, Mr. Avrith,
lied, Mr. Avrith behaved in the same way.

[
67
]

During the hearing before the undersigned, Mr.
Avrith had no hesitation testifying that Mr. Ayoub had lied to Judge
Quenneville in the Small Claims Court
[11]
,
concerning the number of persons Mr. Ayoub's company employed, despite the fact
that Mr. Avrith had heard the explanation given by Mr. Ayoub to Judge
Quenneville.

[
68
]

Given the testimony, exhibits and transcripts,
and the parties' respective accusations of lying, this Court does not consider
that Mr. Ayoub committed any wrongful act during the hearing of February 19,
2007 before the Small Claims Division.

[
69
]

Moreover, even had the Court concluded
otherwise, Mr. Avrith has not shown what damages he suffered. He contends that
Mr. Ayoub's remarks constituted an attack on his reputation. There is no
evidence as to who was present in the Courtroom. Mr. Avrith testified that
the room was full; the parties were waiting for their hearing but he did not
identify any one in the room.

[
70
]

There is no evidence that the mention of a
complaint against Mr. Avrith before the Bar, or even the allegation raised, discredited
Mr. Avrith in the eyes of the parties waiting for trial, who he did not know
and is unlikely to ever see again.

[
71
]

Mr. Avrith only praticed law for two years and
for the rest of his career he has managed his brother's properties. There is no
evidence that the words pronounced in Court impacted on his employment, his
revenue or even his reputation.

[
72
]

In light of the foregoing, the Court cannot
award Mr. Avrith any compensation.

[
73
]

Finally, as obiter, the Court notes that Mr.
Avrith and Mr. Ayoub had been friends. Their relationship went sour. They both
appear to be capable businessmen. They also appear to be stubborn, with neither
wishing to lose face.

[
74
]

Over the past number of years, they have been
involved in several lawsuits and cross demands against each other; the
animosity between them has steadily increased. This case was heard at the same
time as another action instituted by Phillip Avrith Investments Inc. against
3097-1238 Québec inc. (Les Modes J. M.) and Paul Ayoub
[12]
and a cross demand which was presented by
Defendants 3097-1238 Québec inc. and Paul Ayoub.

While the origin of their respective cases is
unclear, their confrontation in Court will not offer either party a solution to
their anger and resentment towards each other. In all probability, mediation
would have produced a far better result and it is unfortunate that the parties
did not opt for that method of resolving their differences.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

DISMISSES
, Plaintiff's action;
